title: Coroner's inquest: Cop recalls chaos in Old South home before fatal shooting
article: There was commotion and confusion inside Samuel Maloney's house when London police raided it eight years ago, an inquest heard.

The jury at the coroner's inquest on Wednesday heard police radio communication from the raid and a first-hand account from Sgt. Jeremy Elliott, one of 11 members of the emergency response unit who descended on Maloney's Old South home on Dec. 23, 2016.

Details about the deadly encounter inside 56 Duchess Ave. were previously revealed through reports from the Special Investigations Unit and London police, a lawsuit and a court case. But Elliott is the first police officer involved to speak publicly about what happened.

Police decided to a conduct a dynamic entry - a tactical police manoeuvre that involves quickly forcing their way into a location and securing it - at 6:05 a.m. to arrest Maloney and seize evidence as part of a probe into the unauthorized use of the Hyland Cinema's website and email.

Elliott said he entered the house through the front door and moved to secure a front office. After finding the room empty, he turned his attention to a second office, where he saw Maloney's common-law wife, Melissa Facciolo, on the ground trying to hold a door shut.
"There was a ton of commotion and yelling throughout the residence. I thought I heard gunshots. It looked to me like one of my teammates was in a position to have taken gunshots," he said.
"So at that point I called 'shot out,' which is a term that we use to say that police have taken a shot or shots."

Elliott said he saw Const. Doug Brown standing in the now-open doorway to the second office, with his rifle pointing into the room. Kids screams mixed with shouting from police officers, Maloney and Facciolo.

"We now know that Mr. Maloney had fired a crossbow at one of our members," Elliott said. "I decided to go back to the truck to get some shields to provide some additional cover and perhaps be used to get other people in the house out, if we needed to do that."
Elliott heard several more "pops" in quick succession while he was outside and assumed it was more police gunfire, he said, adding a call went out over the radio saying the subject was down.

Officers urged a belligerent Facciolo to leave the house so police could search it and she asked for her green winter jacket. Elliott searched the coat and found a folding knife inside a pocket, he said, adding he removed it and handed her the jacket.
The radio communications confirmed Elliott's version of events and added additional insights.
Brown was identified as the officer struck by the crossbow. He negotiated with Maloney, who was demanding police show him their warrant, and asked whether he needed an ambulance.
"He says yes, unknown injuries at this time," Brown said.
Another officer said Maloney had a handgun in his hand, a claim that was later proved to be incorrect after police searched the house.
"We have the female and some babies in the back bedroom and we can't move them," Const. Josh Silcox said shortly before an update goes out over the radio saying "shots fired."
"Subject is down. We're continuing to clear the residence. Female is out with kids," Sgt. Scot Chantler said.
Paramedics were called to the scene as Facciolo can be heard screaming.
Maloney died from gunshot wounds to the head and chest, according to a post-mortem report.

A lawyer for the litigation guardian for Maloney and Facciolo's children grilled Elliott, who drafted the operational plan for the raid, about whether police did enough to safeguard the children inside the home.

Elliott said the children's presence was highlighted in his operational plan presented to tactical officers prior to the raid. The 30-page document also mentioned Maloney was known to keep weapons in the house and had a history of violence and run-ins with police.
The virtual inquest, which is expected to last 15 days, continues Thursday. A jury will make non-binding recommendations to prevent similar deaths.
